taxonomyNote: Feldman and Hoyer (2010) split C. tenuis into two species, C. tenuis and C. longicauda, so older sources (including Animal Diversity Web) describe both as 'sharp-tailed snake'.
fieldMarks: Diminutive snake, usually under 12 in (most about 30 cm), rarely over 16 in; shiny reddish-brown or grey above with indistinct reddish stripes.
Belly has alternating black and cream or pale bars (in Washington the only snake with such bands).
Short tail ends in a small spike-like scale, occasionally lost to injury; smooth scales in 15 rows.
Young snakes are redder with more distinct side lines.
behavior: Small and secretive; under cover in moist rotting logs, stumps, talus and rocks, often near streams, and sometimes several share one cover object.
Surface activity is mostly in cool, moist spring and fall and the rainy season (October-April), with retreat underground in dry summers.
Feeds mainly on slugs, using long re-curved teeth; breeds April-May, lays eggs late June-July and they hatch in fall.
habitat: Edges of coniferous or open hardwood forest, oak woodland, meadows, pasture and broken chaparral; in Washington also riparian floodplains and shrub-steppe with woody debris and rocks.
range: Southern Vancouver Island and Gulf Islands (British Columbia) south through Washington, Oregon and northern California, including the Sierra foothills; in Washington it occurs in about thirteen disjunct areas.

lookalikes.name: Forest sharp-tailed snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Forest sharp-tailed snake has a longer tail with more subcaudal scales (43-58 versus 24-42 in this species).
